title: The ordeal bean becomes a drug

confidence.note: Christison's 1855 paper, Fraser's 1863 account of the ordeal and the later chemical and ophthalmic papers are all dated publications. The ordeal death toll is a missionary estimate and an Edinburgh physician's report, not a count.

summary: A poison used to try the accused in Old Calabar became, via an Edinburgh toxicologist who ate one, a glaucoma drug and a milestone in synthetic chemistry.
body: In Old Calabar, in today's southeastern Nigeria, people accused of witchcraft or crimes were made to eat the seeds of a local vine, called *esere*: vomiting declared them innocent, death proved them guilty. Missionaries who arrived in 1846 estimated it killed some 120 people a year, and beans soon reached Scotland. In 1855 the Edinburgh toxicologist Robert Christison ate part of one and recorded the effects. Its alkaloid, physostigmine, was isolated in 1864, and from 1876 it was used to lower the pressure in eyes with glaucoma. In 1935 the Black chemist Percy Julian synthesized it.

title: A Caesarean section in Bunyoro

confidence.note: The operation is known from Robert Felkin's own report, published five years later in an Edinburgh journal; none of the sources consulted cites a second witness. Felkin's phrasing, as paraphrased, speaks of 'Uganda', while later writers place the operation in the Bunyoro kingdom.

people: Robert W. Felkin (1853–1926), British medical student and eyewitness
An unnamed Banyoro healer and his assistants
summary: In 1879 a British medical student watched an African healer deliver a baby by Caesarean section, and saw the mother recover.
body: In 1879 Robert Felkin, a British medical student traveling with a missionary expedition, watched a healer at Kahura, in the kingdom of Bunyoro in western Uganda, deliver a baby by Caesarean section. The woman was sedated with banana wine, which was also used to wash her belly and the operator's hands; bleeding was seared with a red-hot iron, and the wound closed with seven iron pins. Felkin followed mother and child for 11 days and found the wound healed. In his report, published in 1884, Felkin described the operation as well established in Uganda rather than a rarity; the details here all come from that account.

links.note: Another African practice reported by visiting Victorian doctors.

title: Medicine in the monastery

confidence.note: The texts of Benedict's Rule and Cassiodorus's Institutions survive and say exactly what is quoted. Their dates are less firm: Benedict's life is known mainly from a single later biography, and the Institutions are dated only to a range of years.

people: Benedict of Nursia (c. 480–543), author of the Rule
summary: "Before all things, care must be taken of the sick": how sixth-century monks made nursing a duty and kept Greek medical books in circulation.
body: The Rule written by Benedict of Nursia, who died at Monte Cassino about 543, gave the sick a chapter of their own: "Before all things and above all things, care must be taken of the sick." Sick monks got a separate room, an attendant, baths and meat. Cassiodorus, whose monastery of Vivarium imitated Benedict's, went further. His *Institutions*, written in the 540s or 550s, told monks who nursed the sick to learn the properties of herbs and to read Dioscorides, Hippocrates and Galen (the last two in Latin translation), but not to put their hope in medicines. Five centuries later Monte Cassino would become a center of medical translation.

title: The school of Salerno

confidence.note: Salerno's physicians are praised from the 10th century, but the early school left few records and its origins are obscure. What is known of Trota and the *Trotula* comes from close study of the manuscripts, which has overturned a long-repeated legend.

people: Alfanus, archbishop of Salerno (d. 1085), patron of Constantine the African
Trota of Salerno (early 12th century), healer and medical writer
summary: A town on Italy's Tyrrhenian coast became one of Latin Europe's most famous homes of medicine, and of a woman healer later garbled into the legend of "Trotula".
body: Salerno, on the Tyrrhenian coast of southern Italy, was famous for its physicians by the 10th century, though records of the early school are very poor. It was not a religious foundation and not a university, since none yet existed. In the 11th and 12th centuries it reached its full scientific standing as one of the best-known centers of medical learning in Latin Europe, fed by new texts: Alfanus, archbishop of Salerno (died 1085), was a patron of the translator Constantine the African.

Salerno also had women healers, mentioned more than five dozen times in 12th- and early 13th-century sources. One, Trota, who lived in the early decades of the 12th century, wrote a *Practica* of cures and is credited with a treatise on treating women. Late in that century the treatise and two anonymous texts were bundled as the *Trotula*, a title later mistaken for a woman's name. The verse health guide *Regimen sanitatis Salernitanum* carried the town's name across Europe in more than 300 editions.

myth.tradition: "Trotula" was an 11th-century woman physician and professor at the medical school of Salerno, often said to be the wife of the physician Johannes Platearius.
myth.record: No woman called Trotula is documented; the name is the title of a set of three 12th-century texts. The real healer Trota lived in the early 12th century, nothing is known of her family, and there was no university chair to hold.

title: Arabic medicine into Latin

confidence.note: Constantine's arrival (c. 1076) and death (before 1098/99) rest on monastic records and admiring biographies, and which texts he translated is still being worked out. Gerard of Cremona's death in 1187 is secure, but counts of his translations vary from 68 to about 80, and his authorship of particular versions is attributed rather than signed.

place: Monte Cassino, Italy, and Toledo, Castile
people: Constantine the African (d. before 1099), translator and monk of Monte Cassino
Gerard of Cremona (1114–1187), translator at Toledo
summary: A Tunisian emigrant monk and an Italian scholar in Toledo turned Arabic medicine into Latin, giving Europe the textbooks it used for 400 years.
body: Around 1076 an Arabic-speaking emigrant from Ifriqiya, roughly modern Tunisia, arrived at the Benedictine abbey of Monte Cassino in southern Italy. Constantine the African, as he signed himself, became a monk there, and before his death, sometime before 1098 or 1099, he became the first person known to render a major body of Arabic medical writing into Latin. His largest project, the *Pantegni*, was a version of al-Majusi's *Complete Book of the Medical Art*; among his patrons was Alfanus, archbishop of Salerno.

As far as scholars can tell, Constantine knew only Arabic and Latin, and needed an editor to polish his Latin. Unlike later translators, he tended to disguise the Arabic origins of his texts, and the main charge of plagiarism against him comes from Stephen of Antioch, who re-translated al-Majusi in the 1120s. Yet a bundle of short texts assembled at Monte Cassino, including Hunayn ibn Ishaq's *Isagoge*, an introduction to Galenic medicine, became the core of medical teaching across Europe for some 400 years.

A second, larger wave came from Spain. Toledo, taken by Alfonso VI of Castile in 1085, offered Arabic manuscripts and an archbishop willing to sponsor translation, and in the second half of the 12th century it became the center of the work. Gerard of Cremona had come to learn Arabic and was there by 1144; by his death in 1187 he had translated somewhere between 68 and about 80 works. Through him Latin readers met most of the major Arabic medical writings, including those of al-Razi and Avicenna, whose *Canon of Medicine* in Latin became the basis of university medical teaching until the 17th century.

This was not simply the recovery of lost Greek learning. Much of what arrived was Arabic synthesis and commentary, and Greek authors often reached Latin through Arabic versions. After about 1300 translation from Arabic almost stopped, resuming only after 1480.

myth.tradition: Constantine was a learned physician who spent years traveling through the East before teaching at Salerno, and the books under his name were his own original works.
myth.record: The travel stories come from his monastery's admiring biographers, whose appraisal of his learning one modern scholar calls over-the-top; another early account calls him a merchant. His major books were translations from Arabic whose authors he often left unnamed.

title: Hildegard of Bingen's medicine

confidence.note: Both works are dated to 1150–1158 by the abbey that preserves her legacy. Authorship of *Causae et curae* is not fully settled: its modern editor, Laurence Moulinier, has suggested that its most blatant astrological passages were not written by Hildegard herself, though known to her and used in her convent.

place: Rupertsberg, near Bingen on the Rhine
people: Hildegard of Bingen (1098–1179), Benedictine abbess, visionary and writer
Laurence Moulinier, modern editor of *Causae et curae*
summary: A Rhineland abbess wrote two books on the healing powers of nature and the causes of disease. How much of one of them she actually wrote is still argued over.
body: Hildegard of Bingen (1098–1179), the Benedictine visionary who founded her own convent at Rupertsberg in 1150, is credited with two medical works dated to 1150–1158. *Physica* describes the powers of nature on the healthy and the sick in nine books: plants, elements, trees, gems, fish, birds, land animals, reptiles and metals. *Causae et curae* sets out the causes and symptoms of diseases and their natural remedies. Laurence Moulinier, editor of *Causae et curae*, has argued that its most blatant astrological material was not written by Hildegard herself. For long stretches afterward, few readers paid her medical writings much attention.

links.note: A contemporary center of medical writing, in a lay setting.

title: The medieval hospital

confidence.note: St Bartholomew's traditional founding year is 1123; its earliest royal charter dates from 1133. Santa Maria Nuova's foundation is given as 1288 by the hospital's foundation and as 1285 in older reference works.

people: Rahere, founder of St Bartholomew's priory and hospital
Folco Portinari, founder of Santa Maria Nuova
summary: St Bartholomew's in London began in 1123 as a religious house offering the poor food and shelter. Nine centuries later it is still a hospital.
body: Many medieval hospitals were religious communities that offered the poor shelter and food at least as much as medical treatment. St Bartholomew's in London, founded with its priory by Rahere and dated to 1123, is the UK's oldest hospital still on its original site. Its first proctor, Alfune, probably spent his days begging food door to door and in the city's markets for the poor it sheltered, and in 1316 the bishop of London reminded its brothers and sisters to look after the sick. In Florence, Folco Portinari founded Santa Maria Nuova in 1288; it claims to be the world's oldest hospital still working.
